question: A support manager is designing a new way of working in which Claude drafts replies to routine tickets. Which two design decisions are sound? Select two.
options: A) Define up front what a good draft looks like, so that drafts can be judged against that bar.
B) Measure the pilot only by how many tickets were drafted, since the volume is the whole point.
C) Let drafts go out unreviewed once the first week of the pilot has produced no complaints.
D) Design the process so that Claude also closes each of the tickets it has drafted a reply to.
E) Keep a human approval step before any drafted reply is sent to the customer who asked.
correct_answers: A) Define up front what a good draft looks like, so that drafts can be judged against that bar.
E) Keep a human approval step before any drafted reply is sent to the customer who asked.
explanations: Correct. Defining what good looks like before delegating is what makes the output reviewable rather than merely plentiful.
Incorrect. Volume with no quality measure rewards output the process was never meant to optimise for.
Incorrect. One quiet week is not evidence of reliability, and removing review is the change most likely to surface publicly.
Incorrect. Closing tickets is an accountable outcome, and bundling it into drafting removes the checkpoint the design needs.
Correct. A customer-facing reply is externally published, so keeping a human approval step in the design is the right call.
